09Chapter 9 · Dealing with Few to No Labels

Dealing with Few to No Labels

Real duniya me aksar aisa hota hai ki labeled data bahut kam ho ya bilkul na ho. Label karna mehenga aur slow kaam hai — har example ko kisi insaan ko padh kar tag karna padta hai. Is chapter me hum seekhenge ki kam labels ya zero labels ke saath bhi achha text classifier kaise banaya jaye.

Problem kya hai?

Ek support team ko socho jo GitHub ya Jira jaise issue tracker use karti hai. Har issue ko tag karna hota hai — issue kis type ka hai, kis product se related hai, kis team ko jayega. Ye kaam automate kar diya jaye to team apna time users ki madad me laga sakti hai. Is chapter ka running example hai Transformers library ke GitHub issues ko tag karna.

Har issue me ek title, ek description, aur kuch labels hote hain. Ek issue ko ek se zyada labels mil sakte hain, isliye ye multilabel text classification problem hai — Chapter 2 wali multiclass problem se zyada mushkil, jahan har tweet ko sirf ek emotion milta tha.

Data kaisa hai?

GitHub REST API se lagbhag 10,000 issues download kiye gaye (9,930 rows, 26 columns). Labels ka distribution bahut imbalanced tha — 65 unique labels, jinme wontfix aur model card sabse common the. Zyada tar issues par zero ya ek label tha. Kuch labels, jaise Good First Issue, description se predict karna lagbhag namumkin hai, isliye kaam ko manageable banane ke liye sirf 9 labels par focus kiya gaya: tokenization, new model, model training, usage, pipeline, tensorflow or tf, pytorch, documentation, examples.

Labeled issues sirf 441 thi, unlabeled 9,489 — matlab labeled data 5% se bhi kam tha. Title aur body ko mila kar ek text field banaya gaya, duplicates hataye gaye (1.88%), aur MultiLabelBinarizer se har label ko 0/1 vector me badla gaya. Balanced train/valid/test splits banane ke liye iterative_train_test_split use hua, kyunki multilabel problem me har label ka balance ek saath rakhna mushkil hota hai.

Training slices — chhote data par test karna

Har method ko alag-alag data size par test karne ke liye training slices banaye gaye: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 samples per label, aur full training set (220 examples). Isse ye pata chalta hai ki kaun sa method kitne kam data me kitna achha karta hai — yehi poore chapter ka experiment design hai.

Baseline pehle, transformer baad me

Har naye NLP project me pehle ek strong baseline banao. Do wajah: (1) ho sakta hai simple rule ya simple model hi kaafi ho, aur transformer deploy karna mehenga aur complex ho; (2) baseline ek reality check deta hai — agar BERT 80% accuracy de aur simple logistic regression 95% de, to model me bug hai. Yahan baseline hai MultinomialNB (Naive Bayes) + CountVectorizer (bag-of-words), jise BinaryRelevance se multilabel banaya gaya — har label ke liye ek alag binary classifier. Metric hai micro F1 (frequent labels par performance) aur macro F1 (sab labels ko barabar weight).

Chapter ka decision tree

Data ki halat ke hisaab se raasta chuno: zero labels ho to zero-shot classification; thode labels ho to data augmentation ya embedding lookup; thode zyada labels ho to fine-tuning; aur bahut saara unlabeled data ho to domain adaptation. Aage ke sections me hum in sab ko ek-ek kar ke dekhenge, aur har baar wahi GitHub issues dataset par test karenge.

Yaad rakho: Kam labeled data ka matlab ye nahi ki kuch nahi ho sakta. Pretrained model ki knowledge, unlabeled data, aur sahi evaluation pipeline se 200 examples me bhi kaam ka classifier banta hai — bas pehle baseline banao, phir aage badho.

09.1Chapter 9 · Dealing with Few to No Labels

Zero-Shot Classification

Zero-shot classification ka matlab hai: bina ek bhi labeled example ke, sirf pretrained model ki madad se text ko classify karna. Ye tab kaam aata hai jab historic labeled data ho hi nahi, ya labels lena bahut mushkil ho.

Trick 1 — Masked language model ko classifier banao

BERT jaise model masked words predict karne ke liye pretrained hote hain. Hum model ko dhokha de sakte hain: text ke baad ek prompt jod do, jaise "The movie is about [MASK]." Model ko jo token sabse likely lage, wahi topic hai. Ek example me film ki description (sher, zebra, giraffe, hippo) ke baad ye prompt diya to model ne top prediction animals diya (0.103), jabki cars ki probability sirf 0.001 thi. Dusri description (vehicles me badalne wale aliens) par ulta hua — cars 0.139, animals 0.006. Matlab model sach me context samajh raha hai, sirf keywords nahi gin raha.

Trick 2 — NLI model se zero-shot classification

Mask wali trick achhi hai, par ek aur behtar tareeka hai: natural language inference (NLI) par fine-tune kiya hua model use karo. NLI me model batata hai ki ek premise se ek hypothesis entailment hai (hypothesis zaroor sach hai), contradiction hai (zaroor galat hai), ya neutral hai. MNLI aur XNLI aise datasets hain jin par ye models train hote hain.

Chaal ye hai: classify karne wala text premise banao, aur hypothesis banao "This example is about {label}." Entailment score batata hai ki text uss label ke baare me kitna hai. Ye har label ke liye ek forward pass me chalao. Transformers me iske liye ready-made zero-shot-classification pipeline hai — multi_label=True set karo to sab labels ke scores milte hain, sirf best wala nahi.

GitHub issues par is pipeline ne new model wale example ko 0.98 score ke saath sahi pehchana. Par dusre labels ko bhi kaafi high scores mile (0.16–0.37), kyunki technical/code wala text MNLI ke training data se bahut alag hai. Domain ka farak zero-shot performance par seedha asar karta hai — sentiment analysis jaise common task par ye pipeline bahut behtar chalti hai.

Threshold ya top-k?

Scores milne ke baad labels kaise chuno? Do tareeke: (1) threshold set karo — threshold se upar wale sab labels lo; (2) top-k — sabse high score wale k labels lo. Experiment me top-1 sabse achha raha (zyada tar issues par ek hi label tha). Threshold sweep karne par micro F1 ke liye best threshold 0.75 (F1 0.46) aur macro F1 ke liye 0.72 (F1 0.42) mila. Threshold bahut low rakho to precision girti hai (zyada galat predictions), bahut high rakho to recall girta hai (kam predictions). 0.8 ke aas-paas sweet spot tha.

Zero-shot vs Naive Bayes — natija

50 se kam labeled samples par zero-shot pipeline baseline ko aaram se hara deta hai. 50 se upar bhi micro aur macro F1 dono me zero-shot aage raha. Ye paradox lag sakta hai — "no labels" wale section me bhi validation aur test set use hue — par wo sirf evaluation ke liye the; model ke parameters ko data se adapt nahi kiya gaya, sirf hyperparameters (jaise threshold) tune kiye gaye. Real project me bhi evaluation ke liye mutthi bhar labeled examples rakhna samajhdari hai.

Zero-shot ko behtar kaise karo

  • Label ke naam: pipeline label ke naam par bahut sensitive hai. Naam me semantic meaning honi chahiye — Class 1 jaise naam se model ko koi hint nahi milta. Alag-alag naam try karo, ya kai naam parallel me chala kar aggregate karo.
  • Hypothesis ka form: default hypothesis "This example is about {}" hai, par tum apni hypothesis bhi de sakte ho — use case ke hisaab se isse performance badh sakti hai.
Yaad rakho: Zero-shot ka matlab "bina training ke classify karo" hai. Masked LM prompt ya NLI entailment score — dono me model ki pretraining knowledge hi kaam aati hai. Label ke naam aur hypothesis ki wording hi tumhare control me hai, aur wahi sabse zyada farak daalti hai.

# hide_output
def zero_shot_pipeline(example):
    output = pipe(example["text"], all_labels, multi_label=True)
    example["predicted_labels"] = output["labels"]
    example["scores"] = output["scores"]
    return example

ds_zero_shot = ds["valid"].map(zero_shot_pipeline)
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
def get_preds(example, threshold=None, topk=None):
    preds = []
    if threshold:
        for label, score in zip(example["predicted_labels"], example["scores"]):
            if score >= threshold:
                preds.append(label)
    elif topk:
        for i in range(topk):
            preds.append(example["predicted_labels"][i])
    else:
        raise ValueError("Set either `threshold` or `topk`.")
    return {"pred_label_ids": list(np.squeeze(mlb.transform([preds])))}
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
def get_clf_report(ds):
    y_true = np.array(ds["label_ids"])
    y_pred = np.array(ds["pred_label_ids"])
    return classification_report(
        y_true, y_pred, target_names=mlb.classes_, zero_division=0, 
        output_dict=True)

09.2Chapter 9 · Dealing with Few to No Labels

Data Augmentation

Jab labeled data bahut kam ho, to ek tareeka hai use badhana — naye synthetic examples banao purane examples ko badal kar. Ise data augmentation kehte hain. Computer vision me ye aasan hai (image ko thoda rotate karo, billi billi hi rehti hai), par text me ek word badalne se matlab poora ulta ho sakta hai.

Text me augmentation kyun tricky hai

Do sawaal dekho: "Are elephants heavier than mice?" aur "Are mice heavier than elephants?" — sirf ek word swap hua, par jawaab ulta ho gaya. Lekin jab text lamba ho (jaise GitHub issues, jo kai sentences ke hote hain), to thoda noise label ko nahi badalta. Isliye augmentation lambi texts par zyada safe hai, chhote sawaalon par nahi.

Do common tareeke

  • Back translation: text ko kisi aur language me translate karo, phir wapas source language me. Isse naye wording wale examples milte hain. Ye high-resource languages par sabse achha kaam karta hai, aur domain-specific words zyada ho to kam. Machine translation models jaise M2M100 se implement hota hai.
  • Token perturbations: text me randomly synonym replacement, word insertion, word swap, ya word deletion karo. Jaise "defeat" ki jagah "kill", ya ek random word insert kar do. Libraries jaise NlpAug aur TextAttack iske recipes dete hain.

Contextual synonym replacement

Book me NlpAug ka ContextualWordEmbsAug use hua, jo DistilBERT ke contextual embeddings se synonym nikaalta hai. Example: "Transformers are the most popular toys" augment karne par "are" ki jagah apostrophe aa gaya. Ye thoda ajeeb lagta hai, par label wahi rehta hai, aur model ko thoda noise dekhne ki aadat padti hai.

Natija — augmentation se kya mila?

Thodi si augmentation se Naive Bayes classifier ka F1-score lagbhag 5 points badh gaya, aur lagbhag 170 training samples ke baad macro scores me ye zero-shot pipeline se bhi aage nikal gaya.

Embedding lookup — bina fine-tuning ke classifier

Ek aur powerful tareeka: pretrained language model ke embeddings ko lookup table ki tarah use karo. Teen steps: (1) sab labeled texts ko model se embed karo; (2) naye text ko embed kar ke nearest neighbors dhoondo (FAISS index se); (3) neighbors ke labels ko aggregate kar ke prediction banao. Isme model ko fine-tune karne ki zaroorat hi nahi — sirf do parameters tune karne hote hain: k (kitne neighbors) aur m (label assign karne ke liye minimum count).

Har text ki single vector representation banane ke liye mean pooling use hoti hai — sab token embeddings ka average, padding tokens ko attention mask se hata kar. Book me Python code par train kiya hua GPT-2 variant use hua, kyunki GitHub issues me bahut code hota hai. Query "Implementing efficient self attention in T5" ke 3 nearest neighbors teeno new model label wale nikle — bilkul sahi. Best setting thi k = 15, m = 5, matlab 15 neighbors me se jo label kam se kam 5 baar aaye use assign karo — ratio m/k lagbhag 1/3 best raha.

FAISS kaise kaam karta hai?

Text search me inverted index hota hai (word → documents), par embeddings continuous vectors hote hain — exact match kabhi nahi milta. FAISS dataset ko partition karta hai: pehle k-means clustering se embeddings ko groups me baanto, har group ka centroid nikalo. Query aane par pehle centroids se compare karo, phir sirf best group ke andar dhoondo. Comparisons n se ghata kar k + n/k ho jate hain, aur best k lagbhag √n hota hai. FAISS GPU bhi use kar sakta hai aur vectors ko compress bhi kar sakta hai. Isi technique se ek bada multilingual corpus banaya gaya tha jisse M2M100 translation model train hua.

Yaad rakho: Augmentation se model ko naye examples milte hain, embedding lookup se pretrained knowledge bina training ke use hoti hai. Dono me domain match sabse important hai — jo model tumhare data ke domain ke kareeb pretrained hai, wahi sabse achha chalega. Alag-alag checkpoints try karna sasta hai, sirf checkpoint ka naam badlo.

Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
def augment_text(batch, transformations_per_example=1):
    text_aug, label_ids = [], []
    for text, labels in zip(batch["text"], batch["label_ids"]):
        text_aug += [text]
        label_ids += [labels]
        for _ in range(transformations_per_example):
            text_aug += [aug.augment(text)]
            label_ids += [labels]
    return {"text": text_aug, "label_ids": label_ids}
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
for train_slice in train_slices:
    # Get training slice and test data
    ds_train_sample = ds["train"].select(train_slice)
    # Flatten augmentations and align labels!
    ds_train_aug = (ds_train_sample.map(
        augment_text, batched=True, remove_columns=ds_train_sample.column_names)
                    .shuffle(seed=42))
    y_train = np.array(ds_train_aug["label_ids"])
    y_test = np.array(ds["test"]["label_ids"])
    # Use a simple count vectorizer to encode our texts as token counts
    count_vect = CountVectorizer()
    X_train_counts = count_vect.fit_transform(ds_train_aug["text"])
    X_test_counts = count_vect.transform(ds["test"]["text"])
    # Create and train our model!
    classifier = BinaryRelevance(classifier=MultinomialNB())
    classifier.fit(X_train_counts, y_train)
    # Generate predictions and evaluate
    y_pred_test = classifier.predict(X_test_counts)
    clf_report = classification_report(
        y_test, y_pred_test, target_names=mlb.classes_, zero_division=0,
        output_dict=True)
    # Store metrics
    macro_scores["Naive Bayes + Aug"].append(clf_report["macro avg"]["f1-score"])
    micro_scores["Naive Bayes + Aug"].append(clf_report["micro avg"]["f1-score"])

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

model_ckpt = "miguelvictor/python-gpt2-large"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_ckpt)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_ckpt)

def mean_pooling(model_output, attention_mask):
    # Extract the token embeddings
    token_embeddings = model_output[0]
    # Compute the attention mask
    input_mask_expanded = (attention_mask
                           .unsqueeze(-1)
                           .expand(token_embeddings.size())
                           .float())
    # Sum the embeddings, but ignore masked tokens
    sum_embeddings = torch.sum(token_embeddings * input_mask_expanded, 1)
    sum_mask = torch.clamp(input_mask_expanded.sum(1), min=1e-9)
    # Return the average as a single vector
    return sum_embeddings / sum_mask

def embed_text(examples):
    inputs = tokenizer(examples["text"], padding=True, truncation=True,
                       max_length=128, return_tensors="pt")
    with torch.no_grad():
        model_output = model(**inputs)
    pooled_embeds = mean_pooling(model_output, inputs["attention_mask"])
    return {"embedding": pooled_embeds.cpu().numpy()}

def get_sample_preds(sample, m):
    return (np.sum(sample["label_ids"], axis=0) >= m).astype(int)

def find_best_k_m(ds_train, valid_queries, valid_labels, max_k=17):
    max_k = min(len(ds_train), max_k)
    perf_micro = np.zeros((max_k, max_k))
    perf_macro = np.zeros((max_k, max_k))
    for k in range(1, max_k):
        for m in range(1, k + 1):
            _, samples = ds_train.get_nearest_examples_batch("embedding",
                                                             valid_queries, k=k)
            y_pred = np.array([get_sample_preds(s, m) for s in samples])
            clf_report = classification_report(valid_labels, y_pred,
                target_names=mlb.classes_, zero_division=0, output_dict=True)
            perf_micro[k, m] = clf_report["micro avg"]["f1-score"]
            perf_macro[k, m] = clf_report["macro avg"]["f1-score"]
    return perf_micro, perf_macro

09.3Chapter 9 · Dealing with Few to No Labels

GitHub Issues Tagger Banana

Ab hum sab methods ko ek saath rakh kar dekhte hain: vanilla fine-tuning, domain adaptation, aur advanced methods. End me ek poora tagger banega jo GitHub issues ko automatically label karega.

Vanilla fine-tuning — BERT ko seedha train karo

bert-base-uncased ko multilabel classification ke liye fine-tune kiya gaya: config.num_labels = 9, problem_type = "multi_label_classification", aur labels ko float type me badla gaya (multilabel loss ko probabilities bhi chahiye hoti hain). Chhota data hone se overfitting ka risk tha, isliye load_best_model_at_end=True aur micro F1 ko best-model metric banaya gaya. Training 20 epochs, learning rate 3e-5, batch size 4. Predictions ko sigmoid se normalize kar ke 0.5 threshold par binarize kiya gaya.

Natija: lagbhag 64 examples se vanilla fine-tuning competitive ho gaya, usse pehle behavior thoda erratic tha — chhote sample me kuch labels ka balance bigad jata hai. Ye dikhata hai ki transfer learning kam data me bhi kaam karta hai, par stability ke liye thoda data chahiye.

In-context aur few-shot learning — prompts se seekhna

Ek middle ground bhi hai: model ke parameters badle bina, prompt me hi examples de do. Zero-shot prompt hota hai "Translate English to French: thanks =>" — model merci predict karega. Few-shot me prompt me kai examples de do, aur bade models in examples se aur behtar seekhte hain — ye ek 2020 ke paper ki famous finding hai. Ek aur tareeka hai prompts aur unke desired predictions par language model ko aur train karna — ek method jise ADAPET kehte hain, jo kai tasks par bade models ko bhi peeche chhod deta hai.

Domain adaptation — unlabeled data ka asli use

BERT BookCorpus aur Wikipedia par pretrained hai, par GitHub issues me code aur technical baatein hain — domain alag hai. Beech ka raasta hai domain adaptation: BERT ko apne domain ke unlabeled data par masked language modeling se aur train karo, phir usi adapted model ko classifier bana kar fine-tune karo. Unlabeled data labeled data se bahut zyada aur sasta milta hai, aur adapted model ko baad me kai tasks (NER, sentiment) ke liye reuse kar sakte ho.

Implementation: DataCollatorForLanguageModeling har batch me on-the-fly 15% tokens ko mask karta hai — har epoch me naye masks milte hain. Special tokens ([CLS], [SEP]) ko loss se hata diya jata hai (return_special_tokens_mask=True), aur masked token ka label uska asli token ID hota hai, baaki sab -100 (ignore).

Advanced methods — UDA aur UST

  • Unsupervised Data Augmentation (UDA): model ki prediction ek unlabeled example aur uske thode distorted version par same honi chahiye. Consistency ko KL divergence se enforce kiya jata hai — supervised loss me ek extra term judta hai. Mutthi bhar labeled examples se BERT, UDA ke saath, hazaron examples par train kiye model jaisi performance deta hai. Nuksaan: augmentation pipeline chahiye aur training slow hoti hai.
  • Uncertainty-aware self-training (UST): pehle teacher model ko labeled data par train karo, phir teacher se unlabeled data par pseudo-labels banao, student ko un par train karo, aur student hi agla teacher ban jaye. Uncertainty measure karne ke liye ek hi input ko dropout on kar ke kai baar model se guzaro — predictions ka variance hi certainty ka proxy hai. Ye method full training data wale models ke kuch percent ke andar pahunch jata hai.

Conclusion — kaun sa method kab?

Koi ek method har jagah best nahi hai. Ye depend karta hai: kitna labeled data hai, kitna noisy hai, data pretraining corpus se kitna kareeb hai. Sahi tareeka hai: evaluation pipeline pehle banao, phir methods ko jaldi-jaldi compare karo. Transformers ki flexible API se sirf checkpoint ka naam badal kar kai models try kar sakte ho — Hub par 10,000+ models hain.

Aur ek practical baat: complex method banane se pehle socho ki kya thoda aur data label karna behtar hai. Kuch sau examples label karna kuch ghanton ya dinon ka kaam hai. Aksar ek chhota, high-quality dataset banana, ek bahut complex method banane se zyada faydemand hota hai.

Yaad rakho: Decision tree yaad rakho — zero labels: zero-shot; thode labels: augmentation + embedding lookup; thode zyada: fine-tuning; bahut unlabeled data: domain adaptation. Aur har step par validation/test set pehle se banao, taaki har method ko fairly compare kar sako.

import time
import math
import requests
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tqdm.auto import tqdm

def fetch_issues(owner="huggingface", repo="transformers", num_issues=10_000, 
                 rate_limit=5_000):    
    batch = []
    all_issues = []
    per_page = 100 # Number of issues to return per page
    num_pages = math.ceil(num_issues / per_page)
    base_url = "https://api.github.com/repos"
    
    for page in tqdm(range(num_pages)):
        # Query with state=all to get both open and closed issues
        query = f"issues?page={page}&per_page={per_page}&state=all"
        issues = requests.get(f"{base_url}/{owner}/{repo}/{query}")
        batch.extend(issues.json())

        if len(batch) > rate_limit and len(all_issues) < num_issues:
            all_issues.extend(batch)
            batch = [] # Flush batch for next time period
            print(f"Reached GitHub rate limit. Sleeping for one hour ...")
            time.sleep(60 * 60 + 1)
            
    all_issues.extend(batch)
    df = pd.DataFrame.from_records(all_issues)
    df.to_json(f"github-issues-{repo}.jsonl", orient="records", lines=True)

from skmultilearn.model_selection import iterative_train_test_split

def balanced_split(df, test_size=0.5):
    ind = np.expand_dims(np.arange(len(df)), axis=1)
    labels = mlb.transform(df["labels"])
    ind_train, _, ind_test, _ = iterative_train_test_split(ind, labels, 
                                                           test_size)
    return df.iloc[ind_train[:, 0]], df.iloc[ind_test[:,0]]

Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
np.random.seed(0)
all_indices = np.expand_dims(list(range(len(ds["train"]))), axis=1)
indices_pool = all_indices
labels = mlb.transform(ds["train"]["labels"])
train_samples = [8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
train_slices, last_k = [], 0

for i, k in enumerate(train_samples):
    # Split off samples necessary to fill the gap to the next split size
    indices_pool, labels, new_slice, _ = iterative_train_test_split(
        indices_pool, labels, (k-last_k)/len(labels))
    last_k = k
    if i==0: train_slices.append(new_slice)
    else: train_slices.append(np.concatenate((train_slices[-1], new_slice)))
        
# Add full dataset as last slice
train_slices.append(all_indices), train_samples.append(len(ds["train"]))
train_slices = [np.squeeze(train_slice) for train_slice in train_slices]

Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
from skmultilearn.problem_transform import BinaryRelevance
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

for train_slice in train_slices:
    # Get training slice and test data
    ds_train_sample = ds["train"].select(train_slice)
    y_train = np.array(ds_train_sample["label_ids"])
    y_test = np.array(ds["test"]["label_ids"])
    # Use a simple count vectorizer to encode our texts as token counts
    count_vect = CountVectorizer()
    X_train_counts = count_vect.fit_transform(ds_train_sample["text"])
    X_test_counts = count_vect.transform(ds["test"]["text"])
    # Create and train our model!
    classifier = BinaryRelevance(classifier=MultinomialNB())
    classifier.fit(X_train_counts, y_train)
    # Generate predictions and evaluate
    y_pred_test = classifier.predict(X_test_counts)
    clf_report = classification_report(
        y_test, y_pred_test, target_names=mlb.classes_, zero_division=0,
        output_dict=True)
    # Store metrics
    macro_scores["Naive Bayes"].append(clf_report["macro avg"]["f1-score"])
    micro_scores["Naive Bayes"].append(clf_report["micro avg"]["f1-score"])
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/09_few-to-no-labels.ipynb)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_metrics(micro_scores, macro_scores, sample_sizes, current_model):
    fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)

    for run in micro_scores.keys():
        if run == current_model:
            ax0.plot(sample_sizes, micro_scores[run], label=run, linewidth=2)
            ax1.plot(sample_sizes, macro_scores[run], label=run, linewidth=2)
        else:
            ax0.plot(sample_sizes, micro_scores[run], label=run, 
                     linestyle="dashed")
            ax1.plot(sample_sizes, macro_scores[run], label=run, 
                     linestyle="dashed")

    ax0.set_title("Micro F1 scores")
    ax1.set_title("Macro F1 scores")
    ax0.set_ylabel("Test set F1 score")
    ax0.legend(loc="lower right")
    for ax in [ax0, ax1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("Number of training samples")
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        ax.set_xticks(sample_sizes)
        ax.set_xticklabels(sample_sizes)
        ax.minorticks_off()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

10Chapter 10 · Training Transformers from Scratch

Training Transformers from Scratch

Ab tak humne data ki kami wale cases dekhe, jahan transfer learning hi sahara tha. Is chapter me ulta extreme hai — data itna zyada hai ki hum apna transformer scratch se train karenge. Target hai ek GPT-jaisa model jo Python code autocomplete kare — iska naam hai CodeParrot.

Scratch se kab train karo, fine-tune kab?

Pretrained model use karne ka matlab hai uska tokenizer bhi use karna. Agar tumhara domain alag hai (legal documents, dusri language, music notes, DNA sequences), to wo tokenizer suboptimal hoga. Jaise jaise tumhara corpus pretraining data ke size ke kareeb aata hai, scratch se train karna attractive ho jata hai — bas compute chahiye. Beech me domain adaptation bhi hai (Chapter 9), par yahan hum poora scratch wala raasta lenge.

Bade corpus ki challenges

Bade datasets aam taur par automatic tareeke se bante hain — koi ek-ek example haath se nahi likhta. Iska matlab content par control kam hota hai, aur bias aur low-quality data ka risk badhta hai. Famous datasets ki jaanch me pata chala: C4 corpus ka bada hissa machine-translated hai (human-translated nahi), stopword filtering ki wajah se African-American English ka content kam ho gaya, "sex" jaise common word hi C4 me absent hone se T5 tokenizer use jaanta hi nahi, BookCorpus me copyright violations aur romance novels ki zyada bharmar hai. Model apne training data ka bias inherit karta hai — GPT (BookCorpus par train) ki generations me romance skew dikhta hai, jabki GPT-2 (Reddit-linked webtext par train) zyada neutral, blog-like likhta hai. Isliye dataset ki documentation aur bias ki jaanch zaroori hai.

CodeParrot dataset — GitHub se BigQuery tak

Python code ke liye GitHub natural source hai — 20 million se zyada repositories. REST API rate-limited hai, isliye Google BigQuery use kiya gaya: bigquery-public-data.github_repos tables se sab Python files nikali gayin (binary nahi, size 1 KB se 1 MB ke beech, license ke saath). Query ne 2.6 TB process kar ke 26.8 million files nikali — lagbhag 50 GB compressed JSON. Download ke liye Google Cloud Storage bucket aur gsutil use hua, ya seedha Hub se clone karo: transformersbook/codeparrot.

Filter karna ya nahi, ye ek design decision hai: thoda noise rakhne se model noisy inputs par robust banta hai, par predictions zyada random bhi ho jati hain. Book me educational purpose ke liye stars ya usage se filter nahi kiya gaya — sab Python files le li gayin. Real project me sochna chahiye: languages balance karna, low-quality data hatana, duplicates nikaalna, copyright dekhna, aur passwords/keys jaisi personal information hatana.

Bada dataset, chhoti machine — memory mapping aur streaming

50 GB compressed, 200 GB uncompressed data RAM me nahi aata. Datasets library ke do features kaam aate hain: memory mapping — dataset disk par Apache Arrow cache file me hota hai, aur library uska read-only pointer RAM ki tarah use karti hai; 183.68 GB ka cache sirf 4,924 MB RAM me load hua, 18,695,559 files ke saath. Streaming — streaming=True se files on-the-fly read hoti hain, na cache file banti hai na zyada RAM lagti hai; dataset IterableDataset ban jata hai (random access nahi, sirf order me read), aur Hub se seedha stream bhi kar sakte ho. Isse lagbhag koi bhi size ka dataset, lagbhag kisi bhi chhoti machine par use ho sakta hai.

Yaad rakho: Scratch se training tab socho jab data pretraining-scale ke kareeb ho aur domain alag ho. Usse pehle dataset ki quality samjho — model wahi seekhega jo data me hai, bias aur galtiyon samet.

10.1Chapter 10 · Training Transformers from Scratch

Apna Tokenizer Banana (BPE)

Pretrained model ka tokenizer dusre domain par kharab perform karta hai. T5 tokenizer ne "sex" word kabhi dekha hi nahi (C4 filtering ki wajah se), isliye use 's' + 'ex' me tod deta hai. CamemBERT (French corpus par train) "being" ko 'be' + 'ing' me todta hai. Common words ka tootna sequence length badhata hai aur context waste karta hai. Isliye CodeParrot ke liye apna tokenizer train karna pada.

Tokenizer train karna vs model train karna

Model training me backpropagation aur weights hote hain; tokenizer training me nahi. Tokenizer sirf ek optimal mapping banata hai — text string se integers ki list tak. Isme chaar steps hote hain: normalization, pretokenization, tokenizer model, aur postprocessing. Train hone wala hissa hai tokenizer model — BPE, WordPiece, ya Unigram jaise subword algorithms.

BPE, WordPiece, Unigram — farak kya hai?

  • BPE: single characters se shuru karo, sabse frequently saath aane wale pairs ko merge kar ke naye tokens banao, jab tak target vocabulary size na mil jaye.
  • Unigram: ulta raasta — bade vocabulary se shuru karo aur kam useful tokens ko hata-te jao jab tak target size na mil jaye.
  • WordPiece: Unigram ka purana version, jiska official implementation kabhi open-source nahi hua.

Kaun sa algorithm behtar hai, ye task par depend karta hai aur clearly decide karna mushkil hai. BPE aur Unigram dono zyada tar cases me reasonable hain.

Tokenizer ki performance kaise naapo?

Kuch metrics hain: subword fertility (per word average kitne subwords bane), proportion of continued words (kitne words kam se kam do tukdon me tute), coverage (kitne unknown ya rare tokens), aur misspelling/noise par robustness. Par ye metrics model ke saath interaction ko ignore karte hain — jaise fertility ko zero karne ke liye saare words vocabulary me daal do, par vocabulary bahut bada ho jayega. Aakhir me sabse achha metric hai downstream model performance.

Byte-level BPE — Ġ aur Ċ kya hain?

GPT-2 ka tokenizer byte-level hai: Unicode ke 143,859 characters ki jagah sirf 256 bytes ka alphabet use hota hai. Har byte ko ek printable Unicode character se map kiya jata hai — space (byte 32) → Ġ, newline (byte 10) → Ċ. Isse BPE algorithm bytes par chal sakta hai aur koi bhi Unicode string encode ho sakti hai. Python code example me ĊĠĠĠ ka matlab hai newline + teen spaces (indentation) — aur yehi Python ke liye zaroori hai, kyunki indentation hi semantics tay karti hai. GPT-2 tokenizer indentation ke consecutive spaces ko alag-alag tod deta hai, kyunki wo code par train nahi hua — uski vocabulary me indentation token hi nahi hai.

Apna tokenizer train karo

train_new_from_iterator() se tokenizer train hota hai: target vocabulary size do, strings ka iterator do, bas. Tokenizer ko poora corpus nahi chahiye — sirf representative sample (lagbhag 1–2 GB, 100,000 documents) kaafi hai, kyunki use sirf frequent letter combinations seekhne hain. Pehle try me vocab size 12,500 rakha: pehle tokens me indentation aur self, or, in jaise Python keywords aaye — achha sign. Par await, finally, nonlocal jaise keywords missing the, aur World/say toot rahe the. Dusri try: vocab 32,768 (8 ka multiple, GPU ke liye efficient) aur 200,000 documents — ab sirf nonlocal missing tha (jo waise bhi rarely use hota hai), aur Hello, World, say single tokens ban gaye. Naya tokenizer GPT-2 tokenizer se lagbhag dugna efficient hai — aadhe tokens me code encode hota hai, matlab 1,024 context window asal me 2,048 ke barabar hai, aur wo bhi faster aur kam memory me.

Yaad rakho: Tokenizer domain ka aaina hai — jo corpus par train hoga, wahi words wo jaanega. Apne domain ke liye tokenizer train karna sasta hai (sirf statistics seekhni hain), par iska asar poore model ki efficiency aur quality par padta hai.

10.2Chapter 10 · Training Transformers from Scratch

Large-Scale Training — Streaming aur Accelerate

Tokenizer ready, dataset ready — ab model train karna hai. Ye chapter ka sabse bada hissa hai: architecture chunna, dataloader banana, aur kai GPUs par distributed training chalana.

Pretraining objective chunna

Teen options the: (1) Causal language modeling — code ka shuru do, aage predict karo. Self-supervised hai, aur seedha code autocompletion se judta hai. Decoder-only architecture (GPT family) best hai. (2) Masked language modeling — noisy code do, original wapas banao. Ye general representations seekhne ke liye achha hai (BERT isi se train hua), par autocompletion se seedha link nahi. (3) Sequence-to-sequence — comments aur code ke pairs banao (regex se alag kar ke), ek se dusra generate karo. Isme encoder-decoder (T5, BART) best hai, aur downstream task hai documentation generation. CodeParrot ke liye pehla objective chuna gaya — causal LM + GPT architecture.

Model initialize karna

Pehli baar from_pretrained() ki jagah from_config() use hua: gpt2-xl ki config li, sirf vocabulary size naye tokenizer ke hisaab se badli, aur fresh model banaya — 1,529.6M parameters (1.5B). Chhota version bhi banaya gaya standard GPT-2 config se — 111.0M parameters — taaki pehle chhote par sab test kar sako, phir bada train karo. Dono ko Hub par push kiya gaya.

ConstantLengthDataset — har sequence poori bhari hui

Model ka context 1,024 tokens ka hai, to har training sequence 1,024 ki hi honi chahiye. Kuch examples chhote, kuch lambe hote hain. Trick: kai examples ko tokenize kar ke EOS token se jod do, phir lambi sequence ko 1,024-1,024 ke chunks me kaat do. Isse aakhir ka chhota tukda hi waste hota hai (lagbhag 1% se kam). Buffer bharne ke liye characters-per-token ka estimate chahiye tha — dataset par measure kiya to 3.62 characters per token nikla. Ye IterableDataset hai: buffer me strings jama karo, tokenize karo, EOS se jodo, chunk karo, yield karo. Padding ki zaroorat nahi, kyunki sab sequences same length ki hain, isliye attention mask bhi nahi chahiye. Shuffle buffer se hota hai (buffer_size), kyunki poora iterable dataset ek saath shuffle nahi ho sakta.

Accelerate — distributed training aasan

Accelerate library se wahi PyTorch training loop distributed setting me chal jata hai, bas kuch changes: Accelerator() banao, accelerator.prepare(model, optimizer, data) call karo, aur loss.backward() ki jagah accelerator.backward(loss) use karo. Wahi code local machine par debug ho sakta hai aur training cluster par bhi — mixed precision aur multi-GPU/TPU sab Accelerate sambhalta hai. Trainer bhi distributed training support karta hai, par Accelerate se training loop par poora control milta hai.

Training loop ki khaas baatein

  • Optimizer: AdamW, cosine learning rate schedule, linear warmup ke saath. Bias aur LayerNorm weights par weight decay nahi lagta.
  • Gradient accumulation: bade batch GPU memory me nahi aate, isliye kai backward passes ke gradients jama kar ke ek baar optimize karo.
  • Gradient checkpointing: bade model ka ek batch bhi GPU me nahi aata tha — checkpointing se memory kam hoti hai, lagbhag 20% slowdown ki keemat par.
  • Evaluation: validation loss aur perplexity (loss ka exponential) track karo. Perplexity kam matlab model behtar predict kar raha hai.
  • Logging: Python logger, TensorBoard, aur Weights & Biases — sirf main process log karta hai, har worker apni alag log file likhta hai.
  • Checkpoints: Hub par har experiment ek nayi branch par, har checkpoint ek commit — wait_for_everyone() aur unwrap_model() se model sync kar ke save karo.

DDP — data parallelism kaise kaam karta hai

Accelerate DataDistributedParallelism (DDP) use karta hai: har GPU ko ek batch milta hai, wo apne local model copy par gradients nikaalta hai, phir sab workers ke gradients average hote hain aur har worker apna model khud update karta hai. Isse GPUs badhane par training lagbhag linearly fast hoti hai.

Training run

Script ka naam codeparrot_training.py — Hub se clone karo, requirements install karo, wandb login, accelerate config, phir accelerate launch codeparrot_training.py. Setup tha: 1 machine, 16 processes (A100 GPUs, 40 GB each), FP16, DeepSpeed nahi. Chhota model train hone me lagbhag 24 ghante, bada model lagbhag 7 din.

Yaad rakho: Bade model ki training me code se zyada infrastructure, logging aur checkpointing matter karti hai. Pehle chhote model par sab kuch test karo — mehenga run ek baar me sahi hona chahiye.

import torch
from torch.utils.data import IterableDataset

class ConstantLengthDataset(IterableDataset):
    
    def __init__(self, tokenizer, dataset, seq_length=1024,
                 num_of_sequences=1024, chars_per_token=3.6):
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.concat_token_id = tokenizer.eos_token_id
        self.dataset = dataset
        self.seq_length = seq_length
        self.input_characters = seq_length * chars_per_token * num_of_sequences
    
    def __iter__(self):
        iterator = iter(self.dataset)
        more_examples = True
        while more_examples:
            buffer, buffer_len = [], 0
            while True:
                if buffer_len >= self.input_characters:
                    m=f"Buffer full: {buffer_len}>={self.input_characters:.0f}"
                    print(m)
                    break
                try:
                    m=f"Fill buffer: {buffer_len}<{self.input_characters:.0f}"
                    print(m)
                    buffer.append(next(iterator)["content"])
                    buffer_len += len(buffer[-1])
                except StopIteration:
                    iterator = iter(self.dataset)

            all_token_ids = []
            tokenized_inputs = self.tokenizer(buffer, truncation=False)
            for tokenized_input in tokenized_inputs['input_ids']:
                all_token_ids.extend(tokenized_input + [self.concat_token_id])
            
            for i in range(0, len(all_token_ids), self.seq_length):
                input_ids = all_token_ids[i : i + self.seq_length]
                if len(input_ids) == self.seq_length:
                    yield torch.tensor(input_ids)

from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter
import logging
import wandb

def setup_logging(project_name):
    logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
    logging.basicConfig(
        format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(name)s - %(message)s",
        datefmt="%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S", level=logging.INFO, handlers=[
        logging.FileHandler(f"log/debug_{accelerator.process_index}.log"),
        logging.StreamHandler()])
    if accelerator.is_main_process: # We only want to set up logging once
        wandb.init(project=project_name, config=args)
        run_name = wandb.run.name
        tb_writer = SummaryWriter()
        tb_writer.add_hparams(vars(args), {'0': 0})
        logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
        datasets.utils.logging.set_verbosity_debug()
        transformers.utils.logging.set_verbosity_info()
    else:
        tb_writer = None
        run_name = ''
        logger.setLevel(logging.ERROR)
        datasets.utils.logging.set_verbosity_error()
        transformers.utils.logging.set_verbosity_error()
    return logger, tb_writer, run_name
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/10_transformers-from-scratch.ipynb)
def log_metrics(step, metrics):
    logger.info(f"Step {step}: {metrics}")
    if accelerator.is_main_process:
        wandb.log(metrics)
        [tb_writer.add_scalar(k, v, step) for k, v in metrics.items()]
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/10_transformers-from-scratch.ipynb)
from torch.utils.data.dataloader import DataLoader

def create_dataloaders(dataset_name):
    train_data = load_dataset(dataset_name+'-train', split="train",
                              streaming=True)
    train_data = train_data.shuffle(buffer_size=args.shuffle_buffer,
                                    seed=args.seed)
    valid_data = load_dataset(dataset_name+'-valid', split="validation",
                              streaming=True)
    
    train_dataset = ConstantLengthDataset(tokenizer, train_data,
                                          seq_length=args.seq_length)
    valid_dataset = ConstantLengthDataset(tokenizer, valid_data,
                                          seq_length=args.seq_length)
    
    train_dataloader=DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=args.train_batch_size)
    eval_dataloader=DataLoader(valid_dataset, batch_size=args.valid_batch_size)
    return train_dataloader, eval_dataloader
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/10_transformers-from-scratch.ipynb)
def get_grouped_params(model, no_decay=["bias", "LayerNorm.weight"]):
    params_with_wd, params_without_wd = [], []
    for n, p in model.named_parameters():
        if any(nd in n for nd in no_decay):
            params_without_wd.append(p)
        else:
            params_with_wd.append(p)
    return [{'params': params_with_wd, 'weight_decay': args.weight_decay},
            {'params': params_without_wd, 'weight_decay': 0.0}]
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/10_transformers-from-scratch.ipynb)
def evaluate():
    model.eval()
    losses = []
    for step, batch in enumerate(eval_dataloader):
        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = model(batch, labels=batch)
        loss = outputs.loss.repeat(args.valid_batch_size)
        losses.append(accelerator.gather(loss))
        if args.max_eval_steps > 0 and step >= args.max_eval_steps: break
    loss = torch.mean(torch.cat(losses))
    try:
        perplexity = torch.exp(loss)
    except OverflowError:
        perplexity = torch.tensor(float("inf"))
    return loss.item(), perplexity.item()
Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/10_transformers-from-scratch.ipynb)
set_seed(args.seed)

# Accelerator
accelerator = Accelerator()
samples_per_step = accelerator.state.num_processes * args.train_batch_size

# Logging
logger, tb_writer, run_name = setup_logging(project_name.split("/")[1])
logger.info(accelerator.state)

# Load model and tokenizer
if accelerator.is_main_process:
    hf_repo = Repository("./", clone_from=project_name, revision=run_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("./", gradient_checkpointing=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("./")

# Load dataset and dataloader
train_dataloader, eval_dataloader = create_dataloaders(dataset_name)

# Prepare the optimizer and learning rate scheduler
optimizer = AdamW(get_grouped_params(model), lr=args.learning_rate)
lr_scheduler = get_scheduler(name=args.lr_scheduler_type, optimizer=optimizer,
                             num_warmup_steps=args.num_warmup_steps,
                             num_training_steps=args.max_train_steps,)
def get_lr():
    return optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr']

# Prepare everything with our `accelerator` (order of args is not important)
model, optimizer, train_dataloader, eval_dataloader = accelerator.prepare(
    model, optimizer, train_dataloader, eval_dataloader)

# Train model
model.train()
completed_steps = 0
for step, batch in enumerate(train_dataloader, start=1):
    loss = model(batch, labels=batch).loss
    log_metrics(step, {'lr': get_lr(), 'samples': step*samples_per_step,
                       'steps': completed_steps, 'loss/train': loss.item()})
    loss = loss / args.gradient_accumulation_steps
    accelerator.backward(loss)
    if step % args.gradient_accumulation_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        lr_scheduler.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        completed_steps += 1
    if step % args.save_checkpoint_steps == 0:
        logger.info('Evaluating and saving model checkpoint')
        eval_loss, perplexity = evaluate()
        log_metrics(step, {'loss/eval': eval_loss, 'perplexity': perplexity})
        accelerator.wait_for_everyone()
        unwrapped_model = accelerator.unwrap_model(model)
        if accelerator.is_main_process:
            unwrapped_model.save_pretrained("./")
            hf_repo.push_to_hub(commit_message=f'step {step}')
        model.train()
    if completed_steps >= args.max_train_steps:
        break

# Evaluate and save the last checkpoint
logger.info('Evaluating and saving model after training')
eval_loss, perplexity = evaluate()
log_metrics(step, {'loss/eval': eval_loss, 'perplexity': perplexity})
accelerator.wait_for_everyone()
unwrapped_model = accelerator.unwrap_model(model)
if accelerator.is_main_process:
    unwrapped_model.save_pretrained("./")
    hf_repo.push_to_hub(commit_message=f'final model')

10.3Chapter 10 · Training Transformers from Scratch

Python Code Autocompletion Model

Model train ho gaya — ab dekho wo karta kya hai. Qualitative analysis (examples dekh kar) aur quantitative evaluation (statistics se) — dono tareeke se jaancho.

Loss curves kya kehti hain

Training loss aur validation perplexity dono continuously neeche gaye, aur loss curve log-log scale par lagbhag linear dikhi. Bada model processed tokens ke hisaab se tezi se converge karta hai, halanki total training time zyada lagta hai. Ye scaling ka pehla sanket hai — bada model kam tokens me zyada seekhta hai.

CodeParrot in action

Generation pipeline me temperature 0.4, top_p 0.95, sampling on — aur first_block() function regex se sirf pehla function ya class nikaalti hai taaki output concise rahe. Kuch examples:

  • Rectangle ka area: prompt def area_of_rectangle(a: float, b: float) par 4 completions me se ek sahi tha — return a * b. Baaki galat the (math.sqrt(a * b), a * b / 2.0).
  • HTML se URLs nikaalna: 4 me se 3 completions sahi the — regex se href wale URLs nikaalne wala code. Sahi wale ko Hugging Face homepage par chala kar test kiya to sahi URLs mile.
  • Python se NumPy: bade model ne mean() function ko np.mean(a) me translate kar diya — chaaron completions sahi.
  • Scikit-learn: random forest wale prompt par 4 me se 3 ne RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=20) sahi banaya; ek ne extra-trees classifier bana diya.

Matlab model aksar sahi karta hai, par hamesha nahi — isliye code generation me multiple completions nikaal kar best chunna common practice hai.

Evaluation — BLEU kyun nahi?

Text generation ka BLEU score code ke liye kharab metric hai. BLEU n-grams ka overlap naapta hai — par code me variable ke naam badalne se program sahi rehta hai, phir bhi BLEU punish karega. Naam predict karna insaan ke liye bhi namumkin ho sakta hai. Code ki quality naapne ka behtar tareeka hai unit tests — jaise OpenAI Codex models ko evaluate kiya gaya tha: kai generations ko unit tests se guzaro aur dekho kitni pass hoti hain. CodeParrot ka HumanEval benchmark par performance model ke blog post me diya gaya hai.

Chapter ka safar — recap

Ek code autocomplete function banane ke liye: pehle BigQuery se 50 GB ka Python corpus banaya, phir Datasets ki memory mapping aur streaming se use handle kiya, phir byte-level BPE tokenizer train kiya jo GPT-2 se dugna efficient hai, aur aakhir me Accelerate se 111M aur 1.5B parameters wale GPT-2 models scratch se train kiye — 200 lines se kam code me. Ab tum sirf pretrained models ko fine-tune karna nahi, balki jab data aur compute ho to scratch se pretrain karna bhi jaante ho.

Yaad rakho: Code generation ko text generation jaise evaluate mat karo — BLEU naam par atak jata hai, unit tests sach batate hain. Aur model ki galtiyon se daro mat: multiple samples lo, best chuno, aur test karo.

Python — notebook code (GitHub: https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks/blob/main/10_transformers-from-scratch.ipynb)
import re
from transformers import set_seed 

def first_block(string):
    return re.split('\nclass|\ndef|\n#|\n@|\nprint|\nif', string)[0].rstrip()

def complete_code(pipe, prompt, max_length=64, num_completions=4, seed=1):
    set_seed(seed)
    gen_kwargs = {"temperature":0.4, "top_p":0.95, "top_k":0, "num_beams":1,
                  "do_sample":True,}
    code_gens = generation(prompt, num_return_sequences=num_completions, 
                            max_length=max_length, **gen_kwargs)
    code_strings = []
    for code_gen in code_gens:
        generated_code = first_block(code_gen['generated_text'][len(prompt):])
        code_strings.append(generated_code)
    print(('\n'+'='*80 + '\n').join(code_strings))

11Chapter 11 · Future Directions

Future Directions

Book ke aakhri chapter me hum aage dekhte hain: transformers ko aur bada kaise banaya jaye, attention ko efficient kaise karo, aur text se aage — images, audio, tables, multimodal — transformers kahan ja rahe hain.

The Bitter Lesson — computation hi jeet-ta hai

2019 ke ek mashhoor essay me ye argument diya gaya tha: AI research ke 70 saal ka sabse bada lesson ye hai ki general methods jo computation leverage karte hain, wo aakhir me sabse effective hote hain. Chess aur Go me human knowledge encode karne wale approaches ko zyada computation wale approaches ne hara diya. Transformers ke saath bhi yahi dikh raha hai — 2021 ke best models (jaise GPT-3) asal me original architecture ke bas scaled-up versions hain, bina zyada architectural changes ke. Model size 2017 se kuch saalon me 4 orders of magnitude badh gaya.

Scaling laws — bigger is better, par kitna?

Scaling laws batate hain ki test loss (cross-entropy) ka compute budget C, dataset size D, aur model size N ke saath power-law relationship hai: L ∝ 1/X^α, jahan α aam taur par 0.05–0.095 ke beech hota hai. Matlab loss curves log-log scale par linear hoti hain. Isse teen conclusions: (1) architecture tweaks se zyada fayda N, C, D ko saath me badhane se milta hai; (2) loss curve ke shuru wale hisse se extrapolate kar ke bade, mehenga model ka loss pehle se estimate kar sakte ho; (3) bade models sample-efficient hote hain — chhote model jitni performance kam training steps me pa lete hain. Ye power-law sirf text me nahi, images, videos aur maths problem solving me bhi dikha hai. GPT-3 ko train karne ki cost lagbhag $4.6 million estimate ki gayi thi — isliye pehle se performance estimate karna bahut keemti hai.

Scaling ki challenges

  • Infrastructure: sainkadon ya hazaron nodes/GPUs manage karna alag skill hai — nodes milenge? Communication bottleneck to nahi? Iske liye specialized engineers chahiye.
  • Cost: GPT-3 size ka ek model train karna kai million dollars ka hai — zyada companies ke bas ki baat nahi. (Ek distributed framework bhi propose hua hai jisse chhote groups mil kar compute pool kar ke pretrain kar sakte hain.)
  • Dataset curation: terabytes text me quality aur bias (sexism, racism) control karna mushkil hai; licensing aur personal information ka bhi dhyaan rakhna hota hai.
  • Model evaluation: downstream tasks par evaluate karna, aur biased/toxic generations ke liye probe karna — time aur resources dono lagte hain.
  • Deployment: sainkadon GB ka model serve karna mushkil hai; distillation, pruning, quantization (Chapter 8) madad karte hain, ya hosted APIs use karo.

Do community projects is direction me kaam kar rahe hain: BigScience — 2021–22 ka ek saal ka research workshop, bada multilingual dataset aur bada language model open me banane ke liye, kai million GPU hours ke budget ke saath; aur EleutherAI — volunteer researchers ka decentralized collective, jiska aim GPT-3 size ka model open-source karna hai, aur jisne GPT-Neo aur 6-billion-parameter GPT-J jaise models release kiye.

Yaad rakho: Scaling sirf "aur layers jod do" nahi hai — compute, data aur model size ko saath me badhana hota hai, aur cost, infrastructure aur bias ki keemat bhi chukani hoti hai. Scaling laws tumhe ye faisla pehle se lene me madad karte hain.

11.1Chapter 11 · Future Directions

Scaling Laws aur Challenges

Self-attention transformer ka dil hai — par iski keemat hai O(n²) time aur memory complexity, jahan n sequence length hai. Lambi documents, speech ya vision par ye bottleneck ban jata hai. Is section me attention ko efficient banane ke do bade tareeke dekhte hain: sparsity aur linearization.

Sparse attention — har pair compute mat karo

Attention matrix ke sirf kuch query-key pairs compute karo, ek predefined pattern ke hisaab se. Atomic patterns hain: global attention (kuch special tokens sab ko attend karte hain), band attention (diagonal band par attention), dilated attention (gaps wali window), random attention (har query ke liye kuch random keys), aur block local attention (sequence ko blocks me baant kar sirf block ke andar attention). Asli models in patterns ko mix karte hain — Longformer global + band use karta hai, BigBird usme random bhi jodta hai. Isse maximum sequence length 4,096 tokens tak pahunch jati hai — BERT se 8 guna zyada. Sparsity pattern data se seekhna bhi mumkin hai — jaise Reformer hash function se similar tokens ko cluster karta hai.

Linearized attention — operations ka order badlo

Attention me similarity function aam taur par dot product hoti hai. Linearized attention me similarity ko ek kernel function ke roop me likha jata hai: sim(Q, K) = φ(Q)ᵀφ(K), jahan φ ek high-dimensional feature map hai. Ab φ(Q) ko sums ke bahar nikaal kar pehle Σφ(K)Vᵀ aur Σφ(K) compute kar lo — complexity linear ho jati hai. Linear Transformer aur Performer jaise models isi idea par bane hain. Ek aur result: operations ko reorder kar ke memory complexity O(n²) se O(log n) tak kam ki ja sakti hai.

Attention efficient kyun zaroori hai?

Ye sirf lambi documents ke liye nahi hai — speech aur vision me sequences bahut lambi hoti hain (audio samples, image pixels). Attention ko efficient banaye bina transformers in domains me scale nahi kar sakte. Isi liye ye research ka itna active area hai: sparsity, kernels, aur naye architectures — sab ka goal ek hi hai, attention ki cost ko n² se neeche lana bina quality khoye. Aur ye kaam sirf speed ke liye nahi hai — lamba context milne se model poori book, poora codebase ya poori meeting transcript ek saath padh sakta hai, jo chhote context wale model ke liye namumkin hai.

Yaad rakho: Attention ki O(n²) cost hi transformers ki sabse badi rukawat hai. Sparse patterns (kaun attend kare) aur linearization (kis order me compute karo) — dono alag tareeke se isi cost ko kam karte hain.

11.2Chapter 11 · Future Directions

Beyond Text — Vision, Speech, Multimodal

Sirf text par train kiye models ki limits hain: text me events ki frequency asli duniya se match nahi karti (reporting bias), common sense rarely likha jata hai, facts reliably store nahi hote, aur dusri modalities (audio, visual, tabular) se koi connection nahi hota. Isliye transformers ab text se bahar nikal rahe hain.

Vision — iGPT aur ViT

iGPT images ko pixel sequences ki tarah dekhta hai aur GPT architecture se agla pixel predict karta hai — partial images ko autocomplete kar sakta hai, aur classification head jod kar classification bhi karta hai. ViT (Vision Transformer) BERT-style hai: image ko chhote patches me kaato, har patch ko linear projection se embed karo (jaise BERT me token embeddings), position embeddings jodo, aur ordinary transformer encoder se guzaro. Pretraining me kuch patches mask kar ke unka average color predict karna hota hai. Standard ImageNet par ViT CNNs se behtar nahi tha, par bade datasets par ye CNNs se zyada achha scale karta hai. Transformers me image-classification pipeline se ViT seedha use hota hai — ek dog ki photo par top prediction "Eskimo dog, husky" (0.64) aayi. Videos ke liye TimeSformer spatial aur temporal attention dono use karta hai.

Tables — TAPAS

Tables me bahut saara company data hota hai. TAPAS transformer ko tables par lagata hai — query aur tabular info ko mila kar answer deta hai, aggregator ke saath (NONE, SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT). Example: book ki contents wali table par "What's the topic in chapter 4?" ka jawaab "Summarization" (NONE), "What is the total number of pages?" par SUM ke saath sahi cells, aur "How many chapters have more than 20 pages?" par COUNT ke saath chapters 1, 2, 3. Ye Pandas commands se bhi ho sakta hai, par natural language me sawaal poochhne se non-technical log bhi data query kar sakte hain.

Speech — wav2vec 2.0

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) spoken words ko text me badalta hai — Siri/Alexa jaisi applications ki buniyad. wav2vec 2.0 CNN + transformer use karta hai aur unlabeled data par pretraining se sirf kuch minutes ke labeled data se competitive results deta hai. Transformers me automatic-speech-recognition pipeline se ek audio sample ki transcription bilkul sahi aayi. Uske baad wav2vec-U aaya jo bina kisi aligned speech-text data ke — sirf alag-alag unlabeled speech aur unlabeled text se, clustering aur GAN training se — speech-to-text model banata hai. Isse low-resource languages ke liye bhi ASR mumkin ho gaya.

Vision + Text — VQA, LayoutLM, DALL·E, CLIP

  • VQA: image ke baare me sawaal-jawaab — LXMERT aur VisualBERT vision features (ResNet se) aur text ko transformer encoder me mila kar answer predict karte hain.
  • LayoutLM: scanned documents (receipts, invoices) ke liye — text, image aur layout, teeno modalities input me, spatially-aware attention ke saath. Lakhon scanned documents par pretrain kar ke downstream tasks par transfer hota hai.
  • DALL·E: GPT architecture se text prompt se image generate karta hai — words aur pixels ko ek hi token sequence mana jata hai.
  • CLIP: 400 million image/caption pairs par contrastive learning — text encoder aur image encoder (dono transformers) embeddings banate hain, aur matching pair ki similarity maximize, baaki ki minimize ki jati hai. Zero-shot image classification ke liye classes ko text se embed karo aur image embedding se compare karo — ek robot ki photo par "a photo of a transformer" ko 0.9557 probability mili. CLIP classes ko text se define karne deta hai, architecture me hardcode nahi karta.

Aage kya? — book ka aakhri message

Transformers scaling se bade ho rahe hain aur naye modalities me phail rahe hain. Seekhne ko aage badhane ke liye: Hugging Face community sprints join karo (datasets, ASR models, JAX projects), apna project banao (koi paper reimplement karo ya transformers ko naye domain me lagao), Transformers me naya model contribute karo, ya jo seekha use blog kar ke dusron ko sikhao — sikhaana hi apni knowledge ka sabse achha test hai.

Yaad rakho: Text sirf shuruaat thi. Wahi transformer architecture — attention + pretraining + transfer — ab images, audio, tables aur inke combinations par bhi kaam karta hai. Jo seekha hai, wo har modality me lagta hai.

Tokenizer Lab — Text ko Tokens me Todo

Tokenizer text ko chhote tukdon — tokens — me todta hai. Alag-alag tokenizer alag tareeke se todte hain: BERT WordPiece use karta hai, GPT-2 byte-level BPE, aur character tokenizer har character ko alag token banata hai. Yahan khud try karo aur dekho ki ek hi sentence teeno tareekon se kaise badalta hai.

Apna text daalo aur tokenizer chuno — dekho tokens kaise bante hain
Tokens yahan dikhenge — har token ek chip ki tarah.
Token count aur token list yahan aayegi.

Dhyaan do: WordPiece unknown words ko ## wale tukdon me todta hai, BPE space ko Ġ se dikhata hai, aur character tokenizer sabse zyada tokens banata hai. Token count jitna kam, utna efficient — par bahut kam tokens ka matlab hai bahut badi vocabulary.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 2 — Text Classification

Attention Lab — Self-Attention Samjho

Self-attention me har word sentence ke har dusre word ko "dekhta" hai aur tay karta hai ki kis par kitna dhyaan de. Alag attention heads alag cheezein dekhte hain — ek head shayad subject-verb relation dekhe, dusra head kisi aur pattern ko. Sentence aur head badal kar dekho ki attention kis taraf jata hai.

Sentence aur attention head chuno — attention weights dekho
Attention heatmap yahan dikhega — gehra rang matlab zyada attention.
Sabse zyada attention kis word pair par hai, ye yahan aayega.

Jaise "it" word ka attention "cat" par zyada jata hai — model samajhta hai ki "it" kis ki taraf ishara kar raha hai. Yehi coreference resolution hai, jo attention se hi mumkin hota hai.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 3 — Transformer Anatomy

L3Interactive Lab

Sentiment Lab — Text Classification

Text classification ka sabse simple example hai sentiment analysis — text positive hai ya negative. BERT jaise model ko classification head ke saath fine-tune kar ke ye kaam hota hai. Apna khud ka sentence daalo aur dekho model kya kehta hai.

Koi bhi sentence likho — model uska sentiment batayega
Sentiment meter yahan dikhega — positive ya negative, kitni confidence ke saath.
Scores yahan aayenge.

Positive words (fantastic, loved) score ko upar le jate hain, negative words (boring, terrible) neeche. Sarcasm ya mixed feelings wale sentences par model confuse ho sakta hai — yehi classification ki mushkil jagah hai.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 2 — Text Classification

L4Interactive Lab

Decoding Lab — Greedy vs Beam vs Sampling

Model agla token predict karta hai, par poora text generate karne ke liye ek decoding strategy chahiye. Greedy har baar best token chunta hai, beam search kai options track karta hai, aur sampling randomness jodta hai. Strategy aur temperature badal kar dekho ki output kaise badalta hai.

Decoding strategy aur temperature chuno — generated text dekho
Generated text yahan dikhega.
Strategy ka asar aur token probabilities yahan aayenge.

Temperature kam (0.1) matlab safe aur predictable output; zyada (2.0) matlab creative par kabhi-kabhi bekaar. Greedy repetitive ho sakta hai, sampling diverse — kaam ke hisaab se strategy chuno.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 5 — Text Generation
← PreviousL3 · Sentiment Lab — Text Classification→ NextL5 · ROUGE Lab — Summary Score Karo
L5Interactive Lab

ROUGE Lab — Summary Score Karo

Summarization ki quality ROUGE score se naapi jati hai — generated summary aur reference summary ke beech n-gram overlap. ROUGE-1 unigrams ka overlap dekhta hai. Apni reference aur candidate summary daalo aur score nikalo.

Reference aur candidate summary likho — ROUGE-1 score dekho
Overlap wale words highlight hokar yahan dikhenge.
Precision, recall aur F1 yahan aayenge.

ROUGE sirf words ka overlap dekhta hai — matlab nahi. Ek summary alag words me wahi baat keh kar bhi kam score pa sakti hai. Isliye ROUGE ko human evaluation ke saath hi use karo.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Summarization

L6Interactive Lab

NER Lab — Entities Pehchano

Named Entity Recognition (NER) text me entities dhoondhta hai — log, organizations, jagah, aur bhi. BERT token classification se har token ko label deta hai (jaise B-PER, B-ORG, B-LOC). Apna sentence daalo aur entities dhoondo.

Sentence likho — model entities highlight karega
Entities rangon ke saath highlight hokar yahan dikhengi.
Entity list aur unke types yahan aayenge.

PER matlab person, ORG matlab organization, LOC matlab location. Ek hi word context ke hisaab se alag entity ho sakta hai — jaise "Apple" company bhi hai aur fruit bhi. Context hi faisla karta hai.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 4 — Multilingual Named Entity Recognition
← PreviousL5 · ROUGE Lab — Summary Score Karo→ NextL7 · Quantization Lab — Size aur Speed
L7Interactive Lab

Quantization Lab — Size aur Speed

Quantization me model ke weights ko kam precision me store karte hain — FP32 se FP16, INT8 ya INT4. Isse model chhota aur fast ho jata hai, thodi si accuracy ki keemat par. Model size aur precision badal kar dekho ki size, speed aur accuracy kaise badalte hain.

Model size aur precision chuno — size aur speed ka trade-off dekho
Model size aur inference speed ka comparison yahan dikhega.
Size (GB), speed aur estimated accuracy yahan aayenge.

7B params FP32 me lagbhag 28 GB hote hain, INT4 me sirf 3.5 GB. Bade model ko INT4 me chalana aksar chhote model ko FP32 me chalane se behtar hota hai — size kam, quality zyada.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 8 — Making Transformers Efficient in Production

L8Interactive Lab

Zero-Shot Lab — Bina Training ke Classify Karo

Zero-shot classification me bina ek bhi labeled example ke text classify hota hai. NLI model text ko premise aur "This example is about {label}" ko hypothesis bana kar entailment score nikaalta hai. Apna text aur apne labels daalo — training ke bina hi classification dekho.

Text aur labels likho — bina training ke classify karo
Har label ka score bar chart ki tarah yahan dikhega.
Scores aur best label yahan aayenge.

Label ke naam badal kar dekho — "positive" ki jagah "happy" likhne se score badal sakta hai. Zero-shot label ke naam par bahut sensitive hota hai, kyunki naam me hi semantic hint hota hai.

SOURCESource: Natural Language Processing with Transformers, O'Reilly, Chapter 9 — Dealing with Few to No Labels

F1End Matter · Interview FAQs

Interview FAQs

NLP aur transformer interviews (current era) ke liye — tokenizer se lekar scaling laws tak, 36 sawaal-jawaab. Har jawaab isi book ke concepts par aadharit hai.

Q01 Tokenizer kya hota hai aur ye zaroori kyun hai?
Tokenizer text ko tokens me todta hai — chhote units jinhe model numbers ki tarah process kar sake. Ye zaroori hai kyunki neural networks ko raw text nahi, integers chahiye hote hain. Tokenizer ka design (word, character ya subword) seedha model ki efficiency aur quality par asar karta hai.
Q02 WordPiece, BPE aur Unigram tokenization me kya farak hai?
BPE chhote units (characters) se shuru kar ke frequent pairs ko merge karta hai jab tak target vocabulary na mil jaye. Unigram ulta kaam karta hai — bade vocabulary se shuru kar ke kam useful tokens hatata hai. WordPiece Unigram ka purana version hai. Kaun sa behtar hai ye task par depend karta hai, dono zyada tar cases me reasonable hain.
Q03 Subword tokenization word-level se behtar kyun hai?
Word-level tokenization me rare ya naye words unknown ho jate hain aur vocabulary bahut badi ho jati hai. Subword tokenization rare words ko jaane-pehchane tukdon me tod deta hai, isliye model unseen words ko bhi handle kar leta hai aur vocabulary manageable rehti hai.
Q04 Self-attention mechanism kaise kaam karta hai?
Self-attention me har token sequence ke har dusre token ko dekh kar apni representation banata hai. Query, Key aur Value vectors se attention scores nikalte hain — score batata hai ki ek token dusre par kitna dhyaan de. Isse model lambe context me dependencies pakad pata hai, bina recurrence ke.
Q05 Scaled dot-product attention me scaling factor kyun hota hai?
Dot product bade dimensions me bahut bada ho jata hai, jisse softmax bahut sharp ho jata hai aur gradients chhote pad jate hain. Isliye dot product ko key dimension ke square root se divide karte hain, taaki gradients stable rahein aur training smooth chale.
Q06 Multi-head attention kya hai aur ye kyun use hota hai?
Multi-head attention me attention ko kai heads me baant diya jata hai, har head alag subspace me alag type ka relationship seekhta hai — jaise ek head syntax dekhe, dusra semantic relation. Aakhir me sab heads ke outputs ko mila diya jata hai. Isse model ek saath kai tarah ki dependencies pakad pata hai.
Q07 BERT aur GPT me kya farak hai?
BERT ek encoder-only model hai jo bidirectional context use karta hai aur masked language modeling se train hota hai — ye classification aur understanding tasks ke liye best hai. GPT ek decoder-only autoregressive model hai jo aage ka token predict karta hai — ye text generation ke liye best hai. Dono transformer par based hain, par unka objective aur architecture alag hai.
Q08 Encoder-decoder architecture kab use karte hain?
Jab input ek sequence ho aur output dusri sequence ho — jaise translation, summarization ya question generation — to encoder-decoder best hai. Encoder input ko samajhta hai, decoder output generate karta hai. T5, BART aur PEGASUS iske examples hain.
Q09 Fine-tuning kya hota hai aur ye kaise kaam karta hai?
Fine-tuning me pretrained model ko apne task ke labeled data par aur train karte hain, usually chhoti learning rate se. Model pehle se language samajhta hai, isliye kam data me bhi achha seekhta hai — ise transfer learning kehte hain. Aam taur par task-specific head joda jata hai aur poora model ya uska hissa train hota hai.
Q10 Pretrained model ko fine-tune karte waqt kin baaton ka dhyaan rakho?
Learning rate chhoti rakho (jaise 2e-5 ya 3e-5), warna pretrained knowledge bhool jayega — ise catastrophic forgetting kehte hain. Overfitting se bachne ke liye validation par best model save karo aur epochs zyada na rakho. Domain alag ho to pehle domain adaptation (unlabeled data par MLM) karo, phir fine-tune karo.
Q11 Named Entity Recognition (NER) kya hai?
NER text me named entities — jaise log, organizations, jagah, dates — ko pehchan kar unhe label karta hai. Ye token classification task hai: har token ko ek label milta hai (jaise B-PER, I-ORG). BERT jaise models token-level representations se ye kaam bahut achhe se karte hain.
Q12 Question answering me extractive aur generative QA me kya farak hai?
Extractive QA me model passage se answer ka span nikaalta hai — start aur end position predict karta hai. Generative QA me model answer khud likhta hai, jo passage me word-to-word na bhi ho. Extractive fast aur factual hota hai, generative zyada flexible hota hai par hallucination ka risk rehta hai.
Q13 RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) kya hai?
RAG me pehle retriever (jaise DPR ya FAISS) relevant documents dhoondhta hai, phir generator (jaise BART ya T5) un documents ko dekh kar answer banata hai. Isse model ko external knowledge milti hai bina sab kuch parameters me yaad rakhe, aur answers zyada factual hote hain.
Q14 Summarization me extractive aur abstractive me kya farak hai?
Extractive summarization me model original text se important sentences chun kar jodta hai. Abstractive summarization me model naye words me summary likhta hai, jaise insaan likhta hai. Abstractive zyada natural lagta hai par facts galat likhne ka risk rehta hai.
Q15 ROUGE score kya measure karta hai?
ROUGE summary ki quality measure karta hai — generated summary aur reference summary ke beech n-gram overlap gin kar. ROUGE-1 unigrams, ROUGE-2 bigrams aur ROUGE-L longest common subsequence dekhta hai. Ye aasan metric hai par sirf overlap dekhta hai, matlab ya factual correctness nahi.
Q16 Text generation me greedy decoding, beam search aur sampling me kya farak hai?
Greedy decoding har step par sabse likely token chunta hai — fast par repetitive ho sakta hai. Beam search kai candidate sequences track karta hai aur overall best chunta hai — behtar quality, slow. Sampling (top-k, top-p) randomness jodta hai, jisse output diverse aur creative hota hai. Temperature se randomness control hoti hai.
Q17 Top-k aur top-p (nucleus) sampling me kya farak hai?
Top-k sampling me har step par sirf top k likely tokens me se sample karte hain. Top-p me un tokens ka set lete hain jinki cumulative probability p tak pahunch jaye — set ka size har step par badalta hai. Top-p zyada adaptive hai kyunki confident step par kam tokens aur uncertain step par zyada tokens milte hain.
Q18 Model distillation kya hai aur ye kab use karte hain?
Distillation me ek bade teacher model ki knowledge ko chhote student model me transfer karte hain — student teacher ke soft probabilities (logits) se seekhta hai, sirf hard labels se nahi. Isse model chhota aur fast ho jata hai, performance zyada kam kiye bina. Deployment ke liye jab size aur speed matter kare to distillation use hota hai.
Q19 Quantization kya hai aur isse kya fayda hota hai?
Quantization me model ke weights ko kam precision me store karte hain — jaise FP32 se INT8 ya FP16. Isse model size 2x-4x kam ho jata hai aur inference fast hota hai, accuracy me thoda sa nuksaan hota hai. Edge devices ya limited memory par deploy karne ke liye ye bahut useful hai.
Q20 ONNX kya hai aur ye deployment me kaise madad karta hai?
ONNX ek open format hai jisme trained model ko export kar ke alag-alag runtime aur hardware par chala sakte hain. Transformers models ko ONNX me convert kar ke optimized inference engines se chalaya jata hai, jo production me speed aur portability dete hain.
Q21 Zero-shot classification kya hai?
Zero-shot classification me model bina kisi task-specific training ke text ko classify karta hai. Ye NLI model se hota hai — text ko premise aur "This example is about {label}" ko hypothesis bana kar entailment score se label chuna jata hai. Label ke naam aur hypothesis ki wording performance par bahut asar daalti hai.
Q22 Few-shot learning kya hai aur ye zero-shot se kaise alag hai?
Few-shot me model ko prompt me hi kuch examples de diye jate hain, aur model un examples se pattern seekh kar naya input handle karta hai — bina parameters update kiye. Zero-shot me koi example nahi hota, sirf instruction ya prompt hota hai. Bade models few-shot se zyada fayda uthate hain.
Q23 Data augmentation text ke liye kaise kaam karta hai?
Data augmentation me purane labeled examples ko badal kar naye examples banate hain — jaise synonym replacement, word swap, deletion, ya back translation. Isse model ko zyada diverse data milta hai bina naye labels ke. Dhyaan rakho ki augmentation se label na badle — lambi texts par ye zyada safe hai.
Q24 Embedding lookup se classifier kaise banate hain?
Pretrained model se sab labeled texts ko embed karo, FAISS jaise index me store karo, phir naye text ko embed kar ke nearest neighbors dhoondo aur unke labels se prediction banao. Isme fine-tuning ki zaroorat nahi hoti — sirf k (neighbors) aur m (minimum label count) tune karne hote hain. Best ratio lagbhag m/k = 1/3 hota hai.
Q25 Domain adaptation kya hai?
Domain adaptation me pretrained model ko apne domain ke unlabeled data par masked language modeling se aur train karte hain, phir us par classifier fine-tune karte hain. Isse model tumhare domain ki bhasha aur style seekh leta hai, aur kam labeled data me bhi performance badh jati hai.
Q26 UDA aur self-training (UST) kya hain?
UDA me model ki prediction original aur augmented unlabeled example par same honi chahiye — consistency ko KL divergence se enforce karte hain. UST me teacher model unlabeled data par pseudo-labels banata hai, student un par train hota hai aur phir khud teacher ban jata hai. Dono methods kam labeled data me full-data performance ke kareeb pahunch jate hain.
Q27 Apna tokenizer scratch se train karna kab zaroori hota hai?
Jab tumhara domain pretrained tokenizer ke domain se bahut alag ho — jaise code, legal documents ya dusri language — to apna tokenizer train karo. Pretrained tokenizer common words ko tod deta hai, jisse sequence lambi aur inefficient ho jati hai. Apna BPE tokenizer train karna sasta hai aur model ki efficiency dugni tak badha sakta hai.
Q28 Byte-level BPE kya hai?
Byte-level BPE me text ko Unicode characters ki jagah bytes (256 values) par process karte hain. Har byte ko ek printable Unicode character se map karte hain — space Ġ aur newline Ċ ban jate hain. Isse koi bhi Unicode string encode ho sakti hai aur vocabulary chhoti rehti hai. GPT-2 ka tokenizer isi par based hai.
Q29 Causal language modeling aur masked language modeling me kya farak hai?
Causal LM me model aage ka token predict karta hai, sirf pehle wale tokens ko dekh kar — ye text generation aur autocompletion ke liye hai, GPT isi se train hota hai. Masked LM me kuch tokens ko mask kar ke dono taraf ka context dekh kar predict karte hain — ye understanding tasks ke liye hai, BERT isi se train hota hai.
Q30 Large-scale training me streaming aur memory mapping kyun zaroori hain?
Bade datasets (50 GB ya zyada) RAM me nahi aate. Memory mapping se dataset disk par Arrow cache ke roop me hota hai aur RAM ki tarah access hota hai. Streaming se data on-the-fly read hota hai, bina cache ya zyada RAM ke. Dono se chhoti machine par bhi bahut bada dataset train kar sakte ho.
Q31 Accelerate library kya karti hai?
Accelerate PyTorch training loop ko distributed setting me chalane me madad karti hai — multi-GPU, TPU aur mixed precision, bina code zyada badle. Sirf Accelerator banao, prepare() call karo aur accelerator.backward() use karo. Wahi code local machine par debug aur cluster par train ho sakta hai.
Q32 Gradient accumulation aur gradient checkpointing kya hain?
Gradient accumulation me kai chhote batches ke gradients jama kar ke ek baar optimizer step lete hain — isse bada effective batch size milta hai bina zyada memory ke. Gradient checkpointing me activations ko save karne ki jagah dobara compute karte hain — memory kam hoti hai, lagbhag 20% slowdown ki keemat par.
Q33 Scaling laws kya kehte hain?
Scaling laws kehte hain ki test loss ka compute, dataset size aur model size ke saath power-law relationship hai — loss ∝ 1/X^α. Teenon ko saath me badhane se sabse zyada fayda hota hai, aur chhoti training runs se bade model ka loss predict kar sakte ho. Bade models sample-efficient bhi hote hain — kam steps me wahi performance pa lete hain.
Q34 Self-attention ki O(n²) complexity problem kya hai aur iska hal kya hai?
Self-attention me har token har dusre token se compare hota hai, isliye cost sequence length ke square ke hisaab se badhti hai. Hal hain: sparse attention (sirf kuch pairs compute karo — Longformer, BigBird) aur linearized attention (kernel trick se operations ka order badal kar complexity linear karo — Performer, Linear Transformer).
Q35 ViT (Vision Transformer) kaise kaam karta hai?
ViT image ko chhote patches me kaat kar har patch ko linear projection se embed karta hai, jaise BERT me token embeddings hote hain. Phir position embeddings jod kar ordinary transformer encoder se guzarta hai. Bade datasets par ViT CNNs se behtar scale karta hai.
Q36 CLIP kya hai aur ye zero-shot image classification kaise karta hai?
CLIP 400 million image/caption pairs par contrastive learning se train hota hai — text aur image encoders aise embeddings banate hain ki matching pair paas aur baaki door rahein. Zero-shot classification ke liye classes ko text se embed karo aur image embedding se compare karo — sabse similar class hi prediction hai.
